title: How Married Couples Should Coordinate Roth Conversions
description: Optimizing tax brackets using the 'Joint Filing' advantage.
content:
For married couples, retirement tax planning is a team sport. Filing jointly creates wider tax brackets, allowing you to convert significantly more money from Traditional to Roth accounts at low rates than a single person could. However, this window closes when one spouse dies (the 'Widow's Tax Penalty'). The optimal strategy is to aggressively coordinate Roth conversions while both spouses are alive to minimize the lifetime tax burden of the household and protect the survivor.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Widow's Penalty': When a spouse dies, the survivor files as 'Single'. Tax brackets cut in half. A $100k income that was in the 12% bracket might jump to the 22% or 24% bracket. Converting now protects the survivor later.
  • Bracket Filling: A married couple can realize ~$94,000 of taxable income (2025) and stay in the 12% bracket. If your living expenses are lower than this, 'fill' the rest of the bracket with Roth conversions.
  • The 'One Spender' Strategy: If one spouse retires early, use the drop in household income to start converting the working spouse's Traditional assets, effectively laundering high-income savings through a low-income year.
  • RMD Defense: Converting Traditional assets reduces future Required Minimum Distributions. Since RMDs can push couples into IRMAA (higher Medicare premiums), conversions are a key defense.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The 'Married Filing Jointly' standard deduction is $29,200 (2025). This means the first ~$29k of your conversion is tax-free if you have no other income. This '0% Bracket' is the most valuable space in the tax code.

The Conversion Math

Scenario: Couple, Age 62. Retired. Living on Cash.
Goal: Convert Traditional IRA to Roth before Social Security starts at 70.

The Capacity

Standard Deduction: $29,200.
12% Bracket Top: ~$94,300.
Total Low-Tax Room: ~$123,500.

The Strategy

If they have $0 other income, they can convert $123,500 from Traditional to Roth.

  • First $29,200 is taxed at 0%.
  • Next $23,200 taxed at 10%.
  • Next $71,100 taxed at 12%.
  • Effective Tax Rate: ~9%.

The Win: They moved $123k to Roth paying only 9%. If they waited until RMDs (age 75), that money might have been taxed at 22% or 24%.

Tactical Coordination

  1. Target the Older Spouse: RMDs start at age 73. Convert the accounts of the older spouse first to reduce their RMD balance sooner.
  2. Pay Tax from Taxable: Pay the conversion tax bill using cash from a joint brokerage account. Do not withhold tax from the IRA. This maximizes the amount inside the tax-free Roth shelter.
  3. Watch IRMAA: Conversions count as income. If you convert too much, you might spike your Medicare premiums 2 years later. Check the IRMAA brackets ($206k couple) and stay under.
  4. The 'Deathbed' Conversion: If one spouse is terminally ill, consider aggressive conversions. You still get to file Jointly for that year, using the wider brackets one last time to clean up the tax bill for the survivor.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if we file separately?

Bad idea. Married Filing Separately disallows Roth contributions (income limit is $0) and compresses tax brackets. Almost always better to file Jointly.

Can I convert an inherited IRA?

No. Inherited IRAs cannot be converted to Roth. You must drain them over 10 years. Only your own (or spousal) IRAs can be converted.

Is there a 5-year rule?

Yes. Each conversion has a 5-year clock before you can withdraw the principal penalty-free (if under 59.5). Since you are likely over 59.5, this rule is less relevant, but the account itself must be open 5 years for earnings to be tax-free.
